title: Cloud Storage -- buckets, classes, lifecycle, signed URLs
exp: Cloud Storage is GCP's S3 -- genuinely the closest 1:1 naming match of any storage service across the three clouds, since GCP kept the term 'bucket' itself.
pts: Buckets are globally unique, exactly like S3 -- GCP kept this naming and constraint identical to AWS, unlike Azure's Storage Account + Container two-level structure.

Storage classes: Standard (frequent), Nearline (access ~monthly, 30-day minimum), Coldline (access ~quarterly, 90-day minimum), Archive (rare, 365-day minimum) -- the same cost/access ladder as S3's Standard/IA/Glacier/Deep Archive, with GCP's own naming.
Lifecycle rules auto-transition or delete objects by age, defined as JSON conditions on the bucket -- same purpose as S3 lifecycle rules.
Signed URLs are GCP's presigned-URL equivalent -- time-limited, permission-scoped access generated using a service account's private key or via IAM's signBlob permission.
Object Versioning and Retention Policies protect against accidental overwrite/delete, same purpose as S3 versioning and Object Lock.

Pub/Sub notifications on a bucket (object finalized/deleted events) enable the same event-driven trigger pattern as S3 Event Notifications -- a message published to a Pub/Sub topic the moment a file lands.
code:
from google.cloud import storage
from datetime import timedelta

client = storage.Client()  # uses Application Default Credentials automatically
bucket = client.bucket("satish-pipeline-orders")

# UPLOAD
blob = bucket.blob("2024/01/orders.csv")
blob.upload_from_filename("orders.csv")

# LIST with prefix
for blob in client.list_blobs("satish-pipeline-orders", prefix="2024/01/"):
    print(blob.name, blob.size)

# SIGNED URL -- presigned-URL equivalent
url = bucket.blob("reports/q4.pdf").generate_signed_url(
    version="v4", expiration=timedelta(hours=1), method="GET"
)

# Lifecycle rule -- move to Coldline after 90 days, delete after 365
# (set via gcloud or a bucket.json lifecycle config)
# gcloud storage buckets update gs://satish-pipeline-orders \
#   --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json
#
# lifecycle.json:
# {"rule": [
#   {"action": {"type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "COLDLINE"},
#    "condition": {"age": 90}},
#   {"action": {"type": "Delete"}, "condition": {"age": 365}}
# ]}

r: Bucket -- same term, same global uniqueness

qa.q: Why is Cloud Storage described as the closest 1:1 naming match to S3 of any service across the three clouds?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** GCP kept the term 'bucket' itself and the same globally-unique-name constraint that S3 has -- no intermediate Storage Account layer the way Azure requires. Conceptually and terminologically, gs://bucket-name/object-key maps almost directly onto s3://bucket-name/object-key, making this one of the easiest single mental translations across all three clouds' storage services.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: How does a GCP Signed URL get generated, and what is the practical implication for who can generate one?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A Signed URL is generated using either a service account's private key directly, or via the IAM signBlob permission which lets a caller sign on behalf of a service account without possessing its raw key file -- the latter is the modern, more secure pattern, avoiding key file distribution. The practical implication: whoever's identity generates the signed URL must have appropriate Storage permissions on that object, and using signBlob-based signing (rather than a downloaded key) keeps this consistent with the broader 'avoid long-lived credentials' theme running through every cloud's modern IAM guidance.
